newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil Brady buyback could help risk profile.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil Brady buyback could help risk profile.

text.p: A congressional bill allowing Brazil to swap restructured Brady debt for global bonds promises no quick cash rewards, but it gives the country a powerful tool to defend its risk profile against external shocks, analysts said.
Brazilian Brady bonds, like those of other emerging market nations, are currently trading at record highs which makes any immediate swap unlikely.
"But it is very important to have the option to buy in order to defend Brazil risk," said Dany Rappaport, chief economist for MCM Consultores in Brazil.
"If something happens abroad and Brady prices fall, the government will be able to defend them by buying," he said.

Boosting Brazil's Brady prices narrows their spreads over U.S. Treasuries, which improves the country's risk profile in all global debt markets and makes it cheaper for state-owned firms and corporations to borrow money.
Brazil's Senate on Thursday gave final approval to a Central Bank request to conduct unlimited buybacks of the country's $57 billion Brady debt.

The bonds, made up of restructured commercial bank debt backed by U.S. Treasuries, trade at a discount on the secondary market. They take their name from former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, who helped design a plan under which emerging market countries have been restructuring debt since 1990.
The markets speculate that Brazil already bought some of its debt back to bolster prices, which the government has denied.

There is also talk that Brazil is preparing a $1.0 billion Brady swap with Goldman Dachs, the New York investment bank which led a similar deal for Mexico this year. But analysts say the high price of Brazilian Brady bonds makes such a deal unappealing to policy-makers at this stage.
Brazil's interest in a Brady buyback followed Mexico's successful swap of some $2.3 billion face value Brady bonds for $1.75 billion 30-year global bonds.
In addition to the financial gain of buying back discounted paper, the buybacks also free up U.S. Treasury collateral backing the debt.

Even though Brazil would have to exchange a 5.9 percent coupon on its Bradies for a market coupon of roughly 13.0 percent, the Central Bank has said a deal the size of Mexico's would save Brazil about $200 million.
Some Wall Street economists have scoffed at the idea and say that level of savings is "marginal" compared to Brazil's mammoth $60 billion reserve base.
They suggest Brazil should leave its relatively cheap foreign debt alone and concentrate on slowing growth of its costly $200 billion internal debt stock.
But most Brazilian economists welcomed the Senate approval.

"Internal debt is the main concern. But decreasing external debt by buying back Bradies does not preclude you from concentrating on internal debt," said Nilson Teixeira, chief economist at Rio de Janeiro-based investment bank Fonte Cindam.

Also, some analysts said reducing the stock of restructured debt and replacing it with fresh market-rate paper sends a signal that Brazil is cleaning up its former image as one of the world's largest defaulters.
Teixeira said Brazil could comfortably spend $5 billion to $7 billion of its reserves to buy back Bradies.

If Brazil could follow Mexico's lead and swap Brady debt for fresh 30-year sovereign paper, it would also open the way for state companies and high-grade corporates to issue debt with longer maturities, analysts said.

"It would help build a yield curve which gives issuers a longer term perspective. It also would create a benchmark against which corporates could more easily issue bonds abroad," said a Brazilian economist at a leading international bank, who requested anonymity.
-- Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 232-4411
